title: Did the Wooden Ox Walk by Itself? The Text Says "One Leg, Four Feet" but Gives No Drawing
description:
You've surely heard of the wooden ox and flowing horse: wooden beasts that walked on their own, hauling grain for Zhuge Liang's army. This episode sticks to what's on record and follows them through three years in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (months are lunar): in spring, 2nd month, of Jianxing 9 (231), the army besieged Mount Qi; the Biography of the Later Lord says it "began hauling with the wooden ox", and in summer, 6th month, the grain ran out and the army withdrew. In Jianxing 10 (232), at Huangsha: "the flowing horses and wooden oxen finished; troops drilled". In spring, 2nd month, of Jianxing 12 (234), the army came out of the Xie Valley and "began hauling with the flowing horse"; at the Wuzhang Plains, Zhuge Liang still "always worried the grain wouldn't keep up" and split off troops to farm. Chen Shou's main text says only: "he improved the repeating crossbow; the wooden ox and flowing horse were all his ideas". The sizes are in the Zhuge Liang Ji (Collected Works of Zhuge Liang), quoted in Pei Songzhi's notes: the wooden ox has a "square belly, curved head", "one leg, four feet", "the tongue attached to the belly", "a man goes six chi, the ox four steps" and "carries a year's grain"; the flowing horse has axle holes, leg holes, pole holes, "four legs, front and back" and two square bags. These are part names and hole positions, with no drawing and no complete order of assembly, so these words alone can't settle how many walking legs or wheels it had. Twisting the tongue to stop the device, Sima Yi copying over 2,000 in half a month, and "oxen and horses don't eat" come from a later novel, chapter 102 of Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Where the line falls: hauled grain, filed; what they originally looked like, still open. Ancient units are not converted to kilograms. Sources are listed in the references below (fixed-version transcriptions of the classical texts).

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated story aids, not mechanical reconstructions; the grain haulers in them are always covered with cloth.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

chapters.open-you: Spring 231: the ox at Mount Qi
chapters.wood-018: Retreat from Mount Qi, no totals
chapters.wood-051: Pei Songzhi's note: a square belly
chapters.wood-082: In the novel: a twist of the tongue
chapters.wood-090: A drawing "exactly as the text says"

mn101.text: You've heard of the wooden ox and flowing horse, walking on their own with Zhuge Liang's grain.

mn102.text: Nearly 1,800 years on, the Records of the Three Kingdoms left sizes, not a picture.

mn103.text: In the spring of 231 AD, Zhuge Liang marched out again and laid siege to Mount Qi.

mn104.text: The Biography of the Later Lord has five characters: "began hauling with the wooden ox."

mn105.text: By summer's sixth month, the record says: grain gone, they withdrew.

mn106.text: The new hauler had just set out, and the grain ran out?

mn107.text: That's not the strangest part. A later text says the wooden ox had "one leg, four feet." Did it walk?

mn108.text: In a novel later still, someone twists its tongue.

mn109.text: This file follows three years on record: do the sizes make a picture?

mn110.text: From the histories' words, can we draw their true form?

mn201.text: The same book's Biography of Zhuge Liang also covers it: ox and retreat in one passage.

mn202.text: So does that prove the wooden ox was useless?

mn203.text: No. The books don't say how many were built, or each one's load.

mn204.text: At the front, it wasn't one man who had to eat, but a whole army.

mn205.text: Ever moved house? A great van won't finish the job without enough trips.

mn206.text: Same battle: oxen in use, grain running short. Which number was lacking?

mn207.text: The distance isn't given either, so its total haul can't be worked out.

mn208.text: As the grain officer back then, you'd probably most want a table: sacks per trip, trips a day.

mn209.text: Honestly, on first reading, I was a bit let down.

mn210.text: Then a year later, the histories add one line that muddies it further.

mn211.text: The ox took to mountain roads a year earlier. Why does this line say "finished"?

mn301.text: The difference is one word. At Mount Qi the record says yun, "haul": on the road. This line says bi, "finished": done making.

mn302.text: In Jianxing 10: "the flowing horses and wooden oxen finished; troops drilled."

mn303.text: That year, at Huangsha, Zhuge Liang rested his troops and encouraged farming;

mn304.text: See? One hand builds haulers, the other sends troops to farm and drill: all in one line.

mn305.text: So what got finished: upgrades, new builds, or the last of a batch?

mn306.text: The text lists no count, no steps, nor whether horse and ox were one size.

mn307.text: The text rules out none of the three guesses; my view is, one word, bi, can't carry more than that.

mn308.text: This line adds a name: the flowing horse. At Mount Qi, the year before, only the wooden ox.

mn309.text: It has a name now. But when does the flowing horse finally appear with yun, "haul"?

mn401.text: The answer took two years more. Jianxing 12, spring, 2nd month: Zhuge Liang's army left the Xie Valley.

mn402.text: The Biography of the Later Lord: "began hauling with the flowing horse."

mn403.text: That doesn't mean the very first flowing horse was made that month.

mn404.text: With the flowing horse, you'd think grain kept up this time?

mn405.text: His biography goes on: the army held Wuzhang Plains, at Wugong.

mn406.text: Yet the same passage says Zhuge Liang "always worried the grain wouldn't keep up."

mn407.text: So he split off troops to farm, for a long stay.

mn408.text: Farmer-soldiers lived among locals by the Wei River, fields near the front.

mn409.text: The armies faced off for over 100 days; and every day of it, men had to eat.

mn410.text: Facing off and farming, the front tried to grow some of its own grain.

mn411.text: So which carried the army: the flowing horse, or the farms?

mn412.text: No total for what the horse hauled;

mn413.text: and no harvest table for the farms here either.

mn414.text: So "wouldn't keep up" doesn't show the horse failed, or that it fixed everything.

mn415.text: I think this isn't a magic machine suddenly failing; supply was tight from start to finish.

mn416.text: Notice? This far in, we still don't know if it even had wheels.

mn417.text: They even recorded the grain haulers. Could its shape be on another page?

mn501.text: There is: the main text of the Biography of Zhuge Liang names it, on his ingenuity.

mn502.text: Chen Shou: Zhuge Liang was naturally ingenious; an improved repeating crossbow, the ox and horse, his ideas.

mn503.text: Note: this puts the ox and horse beside the crossbow. As I read it, it praises the man, not the objects.

mn504.text: But the main text ends there, with not one stroke on what it looked like. Where did the details go?

mn505.text: Remember the sizes from the start? Not in Chen Shou's text: in Pei Songzhi's notes.

mn506.text: Pei quotes the Zhuge Liang Ji: "how to make the wooden ox and flowing horse."

mn507.text: It's a note quoting another text, not proof Pei Songzhi measured the device.

mn508.text: The "one leg, four feet" from the start is in the ox part, after "square belly, curved head."

mn509.text: A square belly and a curved head: it does sound like an ox.

mn510.text: But which wooden piece is a "foot"? How does it attach?

mn511.text: The text also says the ox "raises twin shafts": yet another part.

mn512.text: The ox section also says "the tongue is attached to the belly": a tongue, stuck to the belly. Wait, a tongue?

mn513.text: The old text only says such a part sits on the belly; what twisting it does, it says not a word.

mn514.text: As for the four feet, no part is said to flex back and forth; those four characters alone can't show it walked.

mn515.text: And the next line sounds even more like walking: "A man goes six chi, the ox four steps."

mn516.text: Counting man and ox steps side by side: could it really walk by itself?

mn517.text: My reading: "goes" says how far it went; it doesn't show how each joint moved.

mn518.text: Like hearing "this car is fast": you still don't know how many wheels.

mn519.text: Next, the ox "carries a year's grain." Can that be turned into kilograms?

mn601.text: No. It doesn't say for how many people, so there's no sound basis for kilograms.

mn602.text: Honestly, could you say how much rice you eat in a year?

mn603.text: It also says 20 li a day, "and the men are not much tired."

mn606.text: Another line separates two modes: alone, it goes dozens of li; in a group, also 20 li.

mn607.text: Two modes recorded apart: but measured on what road?

mn609.text: It's an old description of hauling, not a test sheet you could follow and repeat.

mn610.text: Then the text switches heading: "Measurements of the Flowing Horse."

mn611.text: As a craftsman out to build it, you'd likely breathe easier: numbers, at last.

mn612.text: The horse section lists the holes one by one, with positions. What are they for?

mn613.text: Axle, leg and pole holes: at least we can tell what kind of part each one takes.

mn614.text: The front axle hole, for instance, is 4 cun from the head and 2 cun across.

mn615.text: Names and numbers like a craftsman's list, not a finished build.

mn616.text: The horse section has legs too: "four legs, front and back." Are they the same part as the ox's four feet?

mn617.text: Can't tell. Ox and horse are written separately, with no word on whether the two sets match.

mn618.text: The horse also has two square bags, each holding 2 hu and 3 dou of rice.

mn619.text: With only this text to build the horse, where does the first joint go?

mn620.text: And the tongue: in the old text, it's just a part attached to the belly.

mn621.text: That hand twisting it at the start: which book is it from?

mn701.text: It's chapter 102 of a later novel, Romance of the Three Kingdoms; there the ox and horse climb hills as if alive.

mn702.text: I guess the walking version you heard as a kid is closest to this chapter.

mn703.text: In the tale, Sima Yi has seized units taken apart, copied to size.

mn705.text: In the novel, an arms race: in under half a month, Wei copies over 2,000 to haul grain at Longxi.

mn706.text: That speed? You can tell it's the storyteller talking.

mn707.text: Shu men in Wei garb slip into Wei's grain column.

mn708.text: Then comes the opening scene: they twist the tongue in its mouth.

mn709.text: It stops dead and won't move. Can the Wei troops drag it off?

mn710.text: Wei troops catch up, can't pull or carry it: right into the novel's trap.

mn711.text: Tongue twisted back, it moves again.

mn712.text: Shu also poses as divine troops with fireworks, so Wei suspects ghosts.

mn713.text: The novel adds four characters: "oxen and horses don't eat."

mn714.text: Are those four in the old text?

mn715.text: That old line only said men weren't too tired; nothing there about not eating.

mn716.text: The tricks are the novel's; the Records of the Three Kingdoms logs hauling, no grain heist.

mn717.text: I like the novel's version too, honestly; far more fun than history.

mn718.text: But shown a reconstruction "exactly as the text says," what should you ask first?

mn801.text: Point to any line on it: which sentence of the text is it from?

mn802.text: Remember the question: where does the horse's first joint go?

mn803.text: Hole names, spacings, yes; but the quote doesn't fully give the assembly order.

mn804.text: Like flat-pack furniture: the manual gives board lengths, but no assembly diagram.

mn805.text: What if someone builds a working grain-hauling model from it?

mn806.text: It only proves that assembly works, not that it was the original.

mn807.text: So two builders, one text: two different-looking devices, and neither defies it.

mn808.text: I think that's more honest: what old books omit, we shouldn't draw in.

mn809.text: Back to the start: from the histories' words, can we draw their true form?

mn810.text: So this file: the wooden ox and flowing horse did haul grain, filed; their true form, still open.

mn811.text: If someone ever finds a real one from back then, I'll gladly reopen this page.

mn812.text: If you drew that text, which part would you want to see first? Tell me.

mn813.text: This channel sticks to the records. Subscribe to open the files with me.
